40.0.s.en: 1. The fall of man and the heavy yoke of sufferings

40.0.0.en: 1 Great travail is created for every man, and an heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day that they go out of their mothers' womb till the day that they are buried in the earth, the mother of all. 2 For they have disturbance of thoughts, and fear of heart, and anxious expectation, and the day of ending. 3 From him that sitteth on the throne in glory, unto him that is humbled in dust and ashes. 4 From him that weareth purple and a crown, unto him that is wrapped in coarse linen. And add to that wrath, and envy, and unquietness, and trouble, and fear of death, and malice, and strife. 5 And in the time of rest upon the bed, the sleep of the night, which troubleth a man's mind. 6 So he hath little rest, as nothing, and afterward in dreams, as in the day of watching. 7 He trembleth at the vision of his heart, as one that fleeth from the face of the battle, and when he escapeth he awaketh and marvelleth that his fear is gone. 8 Such is the lot of all flesh, from man to beast, and sevenfold more for sinners. 9 Death, and blood, and strife, and sword, calamities, and famine, and crushing, and the scourge; 10 all these things were created for the wicked, and for their sakes came the flood. 11 All that is of the earth turneth to the earth again, and all that is of the waters returneth to the sea.

40.0.1.en: Ben Sira presents a lament over what has befallen man in general because of his fall. What was said to Adam: "In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread" (Gen 3:19) has been inherited by all his offspring, so that people feel weariness, even those who are not physically exhausted. Life in the world has become marked by pain, and it ends with the death of the body. During the day man is exposed to the following troubles:

40.1.0.en: a. Confusion about the unknown future and the expectation of death [2].

40.2.0.en: b. Everyone suffers from anger, envy, unrest, anxiety, fear of death, rebellion, and strife [4].

40.3.0.en: c. Even on the bed, for the sake of rest, a man thinks about what befell him in the daytime, and sees it in a form different from what he was thinking [5].

40.5.0.en: e. When he wakes he expects hard things, but he does not find them real [7].

40.5.1.en: Hard labors were created for every man, and a heavy yoke was laid upon the sons of Adam, from the day they came out of their mothers' womb until the day of their return to the mother of all men (the dust) [1].

40.5.2.en: Since human life has become harsh, Ben Sira called it a heavy yoke laid upon the sons of Adam. The book comes to point to the coming of the Messiah, the Savior, who carried the yoke of our sins on the cross, offering to His believers His yoke, saying: "My yoke is easy" (Mt 11:28-30), and some translate it: "My yoke is sweet," since He offers us the sweetness of salvation by the cross.

40.5.3.en: Ben Sira looked at the believers, the children of the new Adam, and saw them moving on toward the mother of all men, as the Apostle Paul says: "But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all" (Gal 4:26). For the Lord Jesus freed us from the yoke of bondage, and granted us the freedom of the glory of the children of God".

40.5.4.en: Man brought upon himself the yoke of sin, so he lost the soundness of his soul and the ability to cleave to the Holy One. He deprived himself of the spiritual bread, the garment of faith was taken off him, and he suffered the wounds of bodily lusts. Man's life was turned into a journey of misery and weariness. "Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble" (Job 14:1). This outlook changed after the coming of the Word of God, for we enjoyed divine grace and sonship to God in the waters of Baptism, and our life became a delightful journey in the company of God. Before the fall there was no conflict between the desires of the spirit and the desires of the flesh; rather, the body and the spirit were in harmony in the love of God and obedience to Him.

40.5.5.en: v "I am a stranger in the earth" (Ps 119:19). I know that "the life of man upon earth is a trial" (Job 7:1), and that "a heavy yoke is laid upon the sons of Adam" [1]. But we say that we are sojourners or strangers on the earth, since we find our city above. Here we receive the pledge, and when we arrive there we shall not depart from it [1].

40.5.6.en: St. Augustine v Of this wrath (which came upon us by the disobedience of Adam) it is said: "We were by nature the children of wrath, even as others" (Eph 2:3). Of this wrath Jeremiah says: "Cursed be the day wherein I was born" (Jer 20:14). And of this wrath the righteous Job says: "Man that is born of a woman is of few days and full of toil. He cometh forth as a flower and is destroyed, and doth not continue in the same state. Upon such a one hast thou set the pupil of thine eye, and me hast thou brought into judgment with thee. Who shall bring a clean thing out of the unclean? No one, even if his life be but one day upon the earth" (Job 14:1-15) LXX.

40.5.7.en: Of this wrath the Book of Sirach also says: "All flesh waxeth old as a garment: for the covenant from the beginning is, Thou shalt die the death" (see Sir 14:17), and also: "Of the woman came the beginning of sin, and through her we all die" (see Sir 35:24). And also: "Great troubles are created for every man, and an heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day that they go out of their mothers' womb till the day of their burial in the mother of all" (see Sir 40:1). Of this wrath the Preacher says: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity. What profit hath a man of all his labour which he taketh under the sun?" (Eccl 1:2-3) [2].

40.5.8.en: v Now the forgiveness of sins relates chiefly to the judgment to come. For in this life what is written is still being fulfilled: "An heavy yoke is upon the sons of Adam, from the day that they go out of their mothers' womb till the day of their burial in the mother of all" [1]. So we see even little children, after they have been washed in the font of the new birth, suffering many evils, and thus we understand that the effect of the sacraments of salvation is suited rather to the hope of the good things of the age to come than to the keeping and possessing of the present goods.

40.5.9.en: Likewise many sins seem now to be overlooked and to pass without punishment, because the punishment for them is reserved for the life to come; so it is not in vain that that day is called the day of judgment, when the Judge of the living and the dead shall come... The Apostle says: "For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged. But when we are judged, we are chastened of the Lord, that we should not be condemned with the world" (1 Cor 11:31-32) [3].

40.5.10.en: v In truth, nothing prevents the fulfillment of the prophecy: "An heavy yoke..." (see Sir 40:1). For even the children who have been set free by the font of regeneration from the bond of sin that held them, that is, original sin, suffer many troubles, and sometimes some of them even suffer the attack of evil spirits. What a joy, that even this attack (God forbid) will not be able to harm them, even if the attack reaches the point of death [4].

40.5.11.en: St. Augustine The awareness of the things to come and of the day of death confuses their thoughts and terrifies their hearts [2].

40.5.12.en: v Death, for those who understand it, is immortality, but for the foolish who do not understand it, it is death. We must not fear this death, but fear the destruction of the soul, which is the ignorance of God. This truly terrifies the soul!

40.5.13.en: v It is impossible for us to escape death by any means. And since the wise truly know this, they practice the virtues and think upon the love of God, and they face death without sighs or fear or tears, thinking that death is on the one hand inevitable, and on the other that it frees us from the sicknesses to which we are subject in this life.

40.5.14.en: St. Anthony the Great From him that sitteth on the glorious throne to the humble one upon the dust and ashes [3].

40.5.15.en: From him that weareth purple and the crown to him that is wrapped in sackcloth. There is wrath, envy, unrest, anxiety, fear of death, rebellion, and strife [4].

40.5.16.en: v Some of those who frequent inns get beds, while others find no beds, so they stretch out on the ground and sleep in perfect peace, just like those who sleep on beds. And in the morning, when the night passes, all rise and leave the inn, each carrying his baggage. So also those who walk in this life: all will leave this life as those who leave an inn, whether they were living a humble life or had wealth and fame. For all of them do not carry with them the earthly pleasures and riches, but take with them what they did in this life, whether good or evil [5].

40.5.17.en: St. Anthony the Great Even in the time of man's rest upon his bed, the sleep of the night changes his knowledge [5].

40.5.18.en: v No one can escape its power, neither slave nor free. All human things perish by death: riches as well as honor. The inequality in this present life is enormous. Great is the freedom after our departure.

40.5.19.en: v Death makes everything void. Not only is there no longer any possibility of supporting evil, but not even the mere sound of evil reaches the ears.

40.5.20.en: St. John Chrysostom He obtains little or nothing of rest, and afterward he sleeps, and behold, he labors in the visions of his heart as in the day of watching, and is troubled by the visions of his heart like one fleeing from the face of the battle [6].

40.5.21.en: And at a certain time he needs to wake up and marvel, since he finds nothing that frightens him [7].

40.6.0.en: This is the lot of all flesh, from man to beast, and for sinners there is sevenfold more: [8]

40.7.0.en: Death, bloodshed, strife, sword, calamities, famine, destruction, and plagues [9].

40.7.1.en: v Death is an exceedingly terrifying thing, but not for those who have learned the true wisdom that is from above. For he who knows nothing of the things to come, but counts death as dissolution and the end of life, rightly trembles and fears, as one passing into non-existence.

40.7.2.en: But he who learns, by the grace of God, the hidden, secret things of the wisdom (of God), and counts it a departure to another place, finds no reason for trembling, but rather rejoices and is glad, since by leaving this perishable life we go to a better, more glorious life without end. This is what Christ teaches us by His actions, going to His sufferings not reluctantly or by necessity, but by His own will; therefore it is said: "When Jesus had spoken these words, he went forth with his disciples over the brook Cedron, where was a garden, into the which he entered, and his disciples" [6].

40.8.0.en: St. John Chrysostom All these things were created for the wicked, and for their sakes came the flood [10].

40.8.1.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that, when the wicked man dies, his sins lead his soul to be the secret of its continual rebuke.

40.9.0.en: All that is of the earth returns to the earth, and what is of the waters returns to the sea [11].

40.9.1.en: v Perhaps you will say: The dead man experiences corruption, and becomes dust and ashes. And what then, beloved hearers? For in this too we rejoice. For when a man rebuilds an old house that is tottering, he first empties it of its inhabitants and tears it down, and then rebuilds it in greater splendor. This causes the inhabitants no grief but rather joy. For they do not think of the destruction that they see, but of the house that is to be built, which they have not yet seen. So also when God does something similar, He brings out the soul dwelling in it as from a house, in order to build a loftier house, and then brings the soul back again in greater glory. Let us not think of the tearing down, but of the loftiness that follows it.

40.10.s.en: 2. A struggle between goodness and evil

40.10.0.en: 12 All bribery and injustice shall be blotted out, but faithfulness shall endure for ever. 13 The goods of the unjust shall be dried up like a river, and shall vanish with noise, like a great thunder in rain. 14 The unjust man rejoiceth when he openeth his hands, but transgressors shall come to nought in the end. 15 The children of the ungodly shall not bring forth many branches, neither shall the unclean roots upon the hard rock. 16 The weed growing upon every water and bank of a river shall be pulled up before all hay. 17 Grace is as a garden of blessings, and mercifulness endureth for ever.

40.10.1.en: Life presents us with a struggle between justice and injustice, and between goodness and evil. But injustice continues for a short time and ends [12]. Faithfulness, however, suffers pains for a while, but it remains forever.

40.10.2.en: All bribery and injustice pass away, but true faithfulness remains forever [12].

40.11.0.en: The wealth of the unjust dries up like a river, and ends like the noise of thunder in the storm [13].

40.11.1.en: Because of the love of money and the desire to increase wealth, man sometimes resorts to deceit, injustice, plunder, and robbery. If a man thinks that injustice is the easy and quickest way to achieve his material gains, does not his heart become corrupt? What injustice brings fades away, but what faithfulness brings, and the straight way that is used, remains to our account in eternity. It is fitting for us that our hand not reach out to bribery and injustice, for the money and possessions that come by way of evil vanish like thunder that appears and disappears in a moment. It dries up as happens with rain water, which spreads quickly and quickly evaporates.

40.11.2.en: v My hope is in God. Yes, for I do not draw near (to evil) but pass by: "Trust not in oppression" (Ps 62:10). In order that I may leap upward, I trust in God; is there then injustice with God?...

40.11.3.en: Injustice may flourish for a while, but it cannot stand. "Trust not in oppression, and become not vain in robbery." You are not rich; do you want to rob? What do you find? And what do you lose? What lost gains! You find money, and you lose righteousness! "Become not vain in robbery"... "Blessed is that man that maketh the Lord his trust, and respecteth not the proud, nor such as turn aside to lies" (Ps 40:4). Yes, you want to deceive; you want to commit fraud, what do you bring upon yourself in exchange for deceit?... For it is neither deceit nor robbery that you desire any longer, nor do you put your trust in these things any longer.

40.12.0.en: St. Augustine The generous man rejoices when he opens his hands, but transgressors (of the commandment) shall perish [14].

40.12.1.en: These words give the believer comfort in the midst of the world's sufferings, for in the midst of evils the believer tastes the righteousness of Christ.

40.13.0.en: The offspring of the wicked shall not put forth branches, for they are unclean roots upon a hard rock [15].

40.13.1.en: The sons of the wicked who walk in the way of their fathers perish because of the evil that they inherited and did not turn away from; they resemble branches that have no root, or whose root has dried up. The children of the wicked are their works (their lack of repentance). When the wicked flourish quickly we grieve over them and weep for them, because the day of their destruction draws near and terrors await them.

40.13.2.en: The sickle of God's justice takes them by surprise, because their life has dried up, and their continuing has become a corruption to the earth. Our teacher James says: "For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways" (Jas 1:11).

40.13.3.en: v "Fret not thyself because of evildoers, for they shall soon wither like the grass." Tell me then, what is the fate of the one who plunders and robs after his departure? Where are his glittering hopes? Where is his awesome name? Does not all this pass away and vanish from existence? Was not all that he had a dream and a phantom?

40.13.4.en: This is what you must expect in the case of such a man, whether during his life or in the life of him who comes after him. But the condition of the saints is not like this, and you cannot utter the same words about their state, nor say that what concerns them is a dream and a legend [7].

40.14.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The harmful weed that grows upon every water or bank of a river is pulled up before all hay [16].

40.14.1.en: v He is like a gardener who uproots the unfruitful plant: "Every plant, which my heavenly Father hath not planted, shall be rooted up" (Mt 15:13).

40.14.2.en: He planted a vine, Sorek,[8] wholly a right seed, and it was turned into bitter and strange shoots[9] (Jer 2:21).

40.14.3.en: He uprooted it in order to make of it a true vine and "God's husbandry" (1 Cor 3:9) [10].

40.15.0.en: Origen Grace is like a garden of blessings, and almsgiving endures forever [17].

40.15.1.en: Who is the generous man but the believer who opens his hands with love and mercy through the work of the Crucified One dwelling in him? He gives love generously, and his heart is turned into a delightful paradise. "Kindness is as a garden of blessings, and almsgiving endures forever [17]. And as he gives, he is enriched by Christ, the Giver of good things; his soul is satisfied, so he feels no want or need, but finds in Him the divine treasure [18]. There is no goodness that passes away, because the blessing of the Lord is upon it. God brings blessings out of evils, as happened with Joseph the son of Jacob.

40.16.0.en: 18 The life of the laborer who is content is sweet, but he that findeth a treasure is above them both. 19 Children and the building of a city continue a man's name, but a blameless wife is counted above them both. 20 Wine and song rejoice the heart, but the love of wisdom is above them both. 21 The pipe and the lute make sweet the melody, but a pleasant tongue is above them both. 22 Thine eye desireth splendor and beauty, but the green of the field is above them both. 23 A friend and a companion meet in accord, but a wife with her husband is above them both. 24 Brethren and help are for the hour of trouble, but the victory of mercy is above them both. 25 Gold and silver make the foot stand sure, but counsel is esteemed above them both. 26 Riches and strength lift up the heart, but the fear of the Lord is above them both. 27 There is no want in the fear of the Lord, neither doth he that hath it need help. 28 The fear of the Lord is as a garden of blessing, and is clothed with glory above all glory. 29 My son, lead not a beggar's life; for better it is to die than to beg. 30 The man that watcheth for a stranger's table, his life is not to be counted for a life, and his soul is polluted with strange meats. 31 The prudent, well-instructed man will beware thereof. 32 Begging is sweet in the mouth of the shameless, and in his belly there burneth a fire.

40.16.1.en: True inner joy is the portion of him who fears the Lord and who is marked by a spirit of discernment in his conduct and works. These inner joys are not everything, but they have their living worth in a man's life. They are blessings that God offers to those who walk in His righteousness. Sirach highlights the superiority of these blessings over ordinary delights:

40.16.2.en: a. The life of the man who is content and who works is sweet, but the inner spiritual treasure is better [18].

40.17.0.en: b. The blessing of begetting children is precious, but a righteous wife without blame is better [19].

40.18.0.en: c. A joyful atmosphere is wonderful, but the love of wisdom is more wonderful [20].

40.19.0.en: d. Spiritual music is sweet, but the pleasant tongue is better [21].

40.19.1.en: e. The eye desires beauty, but the field of the Gospel surpasses it.

40.19.2.en: f. The friend and the companion meet, but the meeting of the wife with her husband is in the heart and never ceases.

40.19.3.en: g. Gold and silver have their role in life, but counsel is a greater treasure than they.

40.20.0.en: h. The fear of the Lord is like a paradise that keeps a man, and there is no glory that equals it [27].

40.21.0.en: i. A man may resort to begging, but death is better than it [28].

40.22.0.en: j. He who desires another's way of living loses his humanity, but the well-instructed man does not desire what belongs to his brother [29].

40.22.1.en: The life of the self-reliant man and of the worker is fragrant, but he who finds a treasure surpasses them both [18].

40.22.2.en: The splendor of life is in earnest work and self-giving, but the treasure that surpasses them is divine grace.

40.22.3.en: Begetting children and building a city establish a name, but the wife who is without blemish is counted better than both [19].

40.22.4.en: As Ben Sira points to the paradisal life through the heavenly Bridegroom, the Lord of glory Jesus, he proclaims the happy married life [19-13] as a shadow of the heavenly wedding. The wife who has no blemish is counted above the children, because she makes them good and gladdens the whole house.

40.22.5.en: Wine and music gladden the heart, but the love of wisdom surpasses them both [20].

40.22.6.en: When the believer hands the steering wheel to wisdom, he enters into a glorious life even in the midst of tribulations, and circumstances, whatever they may be, cannot spoil his inner glory or take away his true dignity. From his young age he bears the marks of the wise elders.

40.22.7.en: v It is Solomon who says that he longs to make wisdom his bride (Wis 8:2). And in another place he says of wisdom: "Love her, and she will embrace you; embrace her, and she will keep you" (see Prov 4:6, 8). Let us also take her for ourselves as a wife! Let us hold her in our arms, and not let her leave our embrace, and we will not let her flee from our arms. If this bride is always in our bosom, we shall beget children from her (that is, the fruit of the Spirit, not of the flesh) [11].

40.22.8.en: St. Jerome The pipe and the harp give sweet rhythm (music), but the pleasant tongue surpasses them both [21].

40.22.9.en: Mar Jacob of Serugh sees that God created man as a praising being, to join the chorus of the heavenly ones.

40.22.10.en: v Men were created to praise much, and perhaps they may remember the praise more every day!...

40.22.11.en: The mouth of man is fashioned as though for the praise of the Lord, and he who ceases from praising becomes ungrateful.

40.22.12.en: Therefore you have a mouth, to praise with it, and to give thanks with it, and to rejoice with it and to bless with it.

40.22.13.en: Praise, because you have the word that praises, and rejoice, because you have the voice filled with melodies.

40.22.14.en: Give thanks, because you have the mind and the discernment, and bless, because you have become a speaking vessel and not a silent one.

40.22.15.en: You were nothing, and mercies made you something great, and since you have come to be, give thanks with wonder; why are you silent?

40.22.16.en: Enter into yourself and look at your person within you, for in you are found all the wonders of the creating power [12].

40.22.17.en: Mar Jacob of Serugh The eye desires grace and beauty, but the green of the fields surpasses them both [22].

40.22.18.en: The eye desires to enjoy the beautiful nature with which God has blessed us, but the green of the fields, which is marked, along with beauty, by fruits of sweet taste, is better. Thus Ben Sira assures the believer that all that God created for us is beautiful, but we must work in the field in order to eat from the labor of our hands.

40.22.19.en: The friend and the companion meet at an appointed time, but the meeting of the wife with her husband surpasses them [23].

40.22.20.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that however close the friendship between two men may be, whether as relatives or colleagues or neighbors, it cannot be compared with the relationship of a man and his wife [13].

40.22.21.en: Brethren and helpers are for days of trouble, but almsgiving delivers better than both [24].

40.22.22.en: Almsgiving is the practice of works of love and kindness, and not merely material giving. By sin man shrinks into selfishness around himself, but by love he is released, by divine grace, from selfishness to work for the benefit and happiness of his brother. For by love we fulfill the whole Law and enjoy righteousness.

40.22.23.en: Gold and silver make the foot stand sure, but counsel is considered more valuable than both [25].

40.22.24.en: Here he urges us to love counsel and to benefit from the wisdom of others more than from gold and silver, as it is said in the Book of Proverbs: "If thou seekest her as silver, and searchest for her as for hid treasures" (Prov 2:4). Is he then calling us to greed or the love of money?

40.22.25.en: v Must we think that the Holy Scriptures praise greed? It is well known what great efforts and pains the lovers of money endure with patience. How they deprive themselves of great pleasures out of desire to multiply their wealth or for fear that it may diminish. With what great violence they pursue gain, and with what great caution they avoid losses... It is fitting that we too be urged thus in the love of wisdom, so that we seek her with utmost zeal as our treasure, seeking more and more, and bearing many troubles, and abstaining from pleasures, and thinking practically about the future so that we may keep purity and the (divine) gift. When we act in this way we acquire true virtues, because our goal is sincere, and agrees with our nature regarding salvation and true happiness [14].

40.22.26.en: v It is not fitting but shameful to compare wisdom with money, yet love is compared with love. What I see here is that all of you love money above everything, so that when the love of money issues a command you spend all your effort to carry it out, and you die of hunger, and cross the sea, and expose yourselves to winds and waves... God says: "Love thus, for I do not ask you to love Me more than this. I am speaking to the common people; I am speaking to the greedy. You love money; then love Me with just such a love and no more. Of course, in comparison (with money) I am better. Love Me as you love money" [15].

40.22.27.en: St. Augustine Riches and strength build up the heart, but the fear of the Lord is better than both.

40.22.28.en: There is no loss in the fear of the Lord, and no need to look for help along with it [26].

40.22.29.en: v Those who look upon the loss of money, or children, or servants, or anything else as a calamity, these must first know the necessity of being content with what God gives, and of being ready to give these things back with composure whenever He asks them of us, without troubling ourselves with grief over losing them, or rather over giving them back, so that we may be like those who use for a time what is not their own and then return it (to its owner) [16].

40.22.30.en: St. Anthony the Great The fear of the Lord is like the paradise of blessing, and it covers a man better than any glory [27].

40.22.31.en: The fear of the Lord offers a pledge of the paradisal life, which we enjoy on earth until we pass over to paradise in the other life.

40.22.32.en: v The Church, for the faithful servants of God, who live in self-control, justice, and love for God in truth, is called a paradise (of blessing), overflowing with abundant graces and pure delights (Song 8:5). Even in tribulation such a servant is glorified in patience and is filled with great joy, because God's consolations delight his soul in spite of the many troubles he experiences in his heart [17].

40.22.33.en: St. Augustine My son, do not live the life of a beggar, for death is better than begging [28].

40.22.34.en: The talk here is directed to the beggars themselves, that they may become producers and not a burden on society. Begging is a disgrace for those able to work. By this he calls us to seek the divine Law earnestly and diligently, instead of begging from the pagan philosophers.

40.22.35.en: v The beggar begs because of his deprivation of what is necessary, and because he finds it impossible to obtain these things in an honorable way. Perhaps in such a case you find those who are said to beg for a cure from the Greeks or the barbarians who promise to offer the truth. They lose the glorious and fitting means offered by the Logos, so they obtain abundant contemplation of the truth without danger. But the Logos forbids this manner of seeking, saying: "Lead not a beggar's life, for better it is to die than to beg" [28].

40.22.36.en: The steward (the manager of affairs) mentioned in the Gospel was ashamed to beg, so he said to the one who owed a hundred measures of wheat: Take thy bill, and write fourscore... (Lk 16:6-7), preferring to reduce the amount of his master's debt rather than to beg in shame, and he was praised for that. Therefore Jesus freed the man born blind from his begging; He gave him sight and granted him the possibility of obtaining what he needed that was necessary for the salvation of his soul (Jn 9:35-38) [18].

40.22.37.en: Origen When a man looks to the table of another, his living is unreasonable, or his way of life is not counted as life.

40.22.38.en: He loses his self-respect by the food of others, but the reasonable, well-instructed man guards against that [29].

40.22.39.en: It is fitting for the believer to eat from the table of his Father, that is, from the Word of God. This table is not strange to us, for we have become members of the household of God (Eph 3:19), instead of begging from the pagans who are strangers to us.

40.23.0.en: In the mouth of the shameless begging is sweet, but in his belly a fire burns [30].

40.23.1.en: He closes the chapter with a warning against folly (shamelessness), for the shameless man begs in order to take, but does not benefit from what he takes, because his inward parts burn with fire [30]. This warning is for those who find begging easier than practicing work, especially the young men able to work.

40.24.0.en: v In my weakness I bowed my shoulder under the heavy yoke of sin.

40.24.1.en: And by Your love I fly, as by the Spirit, toward the heavens, rejoicing!

40.24.2.en: I await the meeting with You, O Giver of joy and rest!

40.24.3.en: You freed me from returning to the dust forever, and lifted me up to the fellowship of the heavenly glories.

40.24.4.en: v As a wonderful commander and a divine trainer You led me into the battle.

40.24.5.en: You drew me to Your goodness, and made sin bitter in my mouth.

40.24.6.en: I find sweet my release from selfishness, that I may practice love with joy.

40.24.7.en: You turned my whole being into a harp that praises You without slackening.

40.24.8.en: Your fear has become a paradise; I enjoy blessings and glories.

40.24.9.en: I no longer beg for the food of the world, for I sit at Your table!

40.24.10.en: What shall I render to You, O Lord, for the multitude of Your mercies and Your love?!
